In mathematics, a '''convergence group''' or a '''discrete convergence group''' is a [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>\Gamma</math> [[Group action (mathematics)|acting]] by [[homeomorphism]]s on a [[compact space|compact]] [[metrizable space]] <math>M</math> in a way that generalizes the properties of the action of [[Kleinian group]] by [[Möbius transformation]]s on the ideal boundary <math>\mathbb S^2</math> of the [[Hyperbolic space|hyperbolic 3-space <math>\mathbb H^3 </math>]].
The notion of a convergence group was introduced by [[Frederick Gehring|Gehring]] and [[Gaven Martin|Martin]] (1987) <ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Gehring | first1=F. W.
| last2=Martin | first2=G. J.
| title=Discrete quasiconformal groups I
| journal=[[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]]
| volume=55
| date=1987
| issue=2
| pages=331–358
| doi=10.1093/plms/s3-55_2.331| hdl=2027.42/135296
| hdl-access=free
}}</ref> and has since found wide applications in [[geometric topology]], [[Quasiconformal mapping|quasiconformal analysis]], and [[geometric group theory]].

== Formal definition ==

Let <math>\Gamma</math> be a group acting by homeomorphisms on a compact metrizable space <math>M</math>. This action is called a ''convergence action'' or a ''discrete convergence action'' (and then <math>\Gamma</math> is called a ''convergence group'' or a ''discrete convergence group'' for this action) if for every infinite distinct sequence of elements <math>\gamma_n \in \Gamma</math> there exist a subsequence <math>\gamma_{n_k}, k=1,2,\dots</math> and points <math>a,b\in M</math> such that the maps <math>\gamma_{n_k}\big|_{M\setminus\{a\}}</math> converge uniformly on compact subsets to the constant map sending <math>M\setminus\{a\}</math> to <math>b</math>.  Here converging uniformly on compact subsets means that for every open neighborhood <math>U</math> of <math>b</math> in <math>M</math> and every compact <math> K\subset M\setminus \{a\}</math> there exists an index <math>k_0\ge 1</math> such that for every <math>k\ge k_0,</math> <math> \gamma_{n_k}(K)\subseteq U</math>. Note that the "poles" <math> a, b\in M</math> associated with the subsequence  <math>\gamma_{n_k}</math> are not required  to be distinct.

=== Reformulation in terms of the action on distinct triples ===

The above definition of convergence group admits a useful equivalent reformulation in terms of the action of <math>\Gamma</math> on the "space of distinct triples" of <math>M</math>.
For a set <math>M</math> denote <math>\Theta(M):=M^3\setminus \Delta(M)</math>, where <math>\Delta(M)=\{(a,b,c)\in M^3\mid \#\{a,b,c\}\le 2\}</math>. The set <math>\Theta(M)</math> is called the "space of distinct triples" for <math>M</math>.

Then the following equivalence is known to hold:<ref name=Bow-config>{{cite book
| last1=Bowditch | first1=B. H. | authorlink1=Brian Bowditch
| chapter=Convergence groups and configuration spaces
| title=Geometric group theory down under (Canberra, 1996)
| pages=23–54
| series=De Gruyter Proceedings in Mathematics
| publisher=de Gruyter, Berlin
| date=1999
| doi=10.1515/9783110806861.23| isbn=9783110806861 }}</ref>

Let <math>\Gamma</math> be a group acting by homeomorphisms on a compact metrizable space <math>M</math> with at least two points. Then this action is a discrete convergence action [[if and only if]] the induced action of <math>\Gamma</math> on <math>\Theta(M)</math> is [[properly discontinuous action|properly discontinuous]].

== Examples ==

*The action of a [[Kleinian group]] <math>\Gamma</math> on <math>\mathbb S^2=\partial \mathbb H^3</math> by [[Möbius transformation]]s is a convergence group action.
* The action of a [[word-hyperbolic group]] <math>G</math> by translations on its ideal boundary <math>\partial G</math> is a convergence group action.
* The action of a [[relatively hyperbolic group]] <math>G</math> by translations on its Bowditch boundary <math>\partial G</math> is a convergence group action.
* Let <math>X</math> be a proper geodesic [[δ-hyperbolic space|Gromov-hyperbolic]] [[metric space]] and let <math>\Gamma</math> be a group acting properly discontinuously by isometries on <math>X</math>. Then the corresponding boundary action of <math>\Gamma</math> on <math>\partial X</math> is a discrete convergence action (Lemma 2.11 of <ref name=Bow-config />).

== Classification of elements in convergence groups ==

Let <math>\Gamma</math> be a group acting by homeomorphisms on a compact metrizable space <math>M</math>with at least three points,  and let <math>\gamma\in\Gamma</math>. Then it is known (Lemma 3.1 in <ref name=Bow-config /> or Lemma 6.2 in <ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Bowditch | first1=B. H. | authorlink1=Brian Bowditch
| title=Treelike structures arising from continua and convergence groups
| journal=[[Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society]]
| volume=139
| date=1999
| issue=662
| doi=10.1090/memo/0662}}</ref>) that exactly one of the following occurs:

(1) The element <math>\gamma</math> has finite order in <math>\Gamma </math>; in this case <math>\gamma</math>  is called ''elliptic''.

(2) The element <math>\gamma</math> has infinite order in <math>\Gamma </math> and the fixed set <math>\operatorname{Fix}_M(\gamma)</math> is a single point; in this case <math>\gamma</math>  is called ''parabolic''.

(3) The element <math>\gamma</math> has infinite order in <math>\Gamma</math> and the fixed set <math>\operatorname{Fix}_M(\gamma)</math> consists of two distinct points; in this case <math>\gamma</math>  is called ''loxodromic''.

Moreover, for every <math>p\ne 0</math> the elements <math>\gamma</math> and <math>\gamma^p</math>have the same type.  Also in cases (2) and (3) <math>\operatorname{Fix}_M(\gamma) = \operatorname{Fix}_M(\gamma^p)</math> (where <math>p\ne 0</math>) and the group <math>\langle \gamma\rangle </math> acts properly discontinuously on <math>M\setminus \operatorname{Fix}_M(\gamma)</math>. Additionally, if <math>\gamma</math> is loxodromic, then <math>\langle \gamma\rangle </math> acts properly discontinuously and cocompactly on <math>M\setminus \operatorname{Fix}_M(\gamma) </math>.

If  <math>\gamma\in \Gamma</math> is parabolic with a fixed point <math>a\in M</math> then for every <math>x\in M</math> one has <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma^nx=\lim_{n\to-\infty}\gamma^nx =a</math>
If <math>\gamma\in \Gamma</math> is loxodromic, then <math>\operatorname{Fix}_M(\gamma)</math> can be written as <math>\operatorname{Fix}_M(\gamma)=\{a_-,a_+\}</math> so that for every <math> x \in  M\setminus \{a_-\} </math> one has <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma^nx=a_+</math> and for every <math> x \in  M\setminus \{a_+\} </math> one has <math>\lim_{n\to-\infty}\gamma^nx=a_-</math>, and these convergences are  uniform on compact subsets of <math>M\setminus \{a_-, a_+\}</math>.

== Uniform convergence groups ==

A discrete convergence action of a group <math>\Gamma</math> on a compact metrizable space <math>M</math> is called ''uniform'' (in which case <math>\Gamma</math> is called a ''uniform convergence group'') if the action of <math>\Gamma</math> on <math>\Theta(M)</math> is [[Cocompact group action|co-compact]]. Thus <math>\Gamma</math> is a [[uniform convergence]] group if and only if its action on <math>\Theta(M)</math> is both properly discontinuous and co-compact.

=== Conical limit points ===

Let <math>\Gamma</math> act on a compact metrizable space <math>M</math> as a discrete convergence group. A point <math>x\in M</math> is called a ''conical limit point'' (sometimes also called a ''radial limit point'' or  a ''point of approximation'') if there exist an infinite sequence of distinct elements <math>\gamma_n\in \Gamma</math> and distinct points <math>a,b\in M</math> such that <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_n x=a</math> and for every <math>y\in M\setminus \{x\}</math> one has <math> \lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_n y=b</math>.

An important result of [[Pekka Tukia|Tukia]],<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Tukia | first1=Pekka
| title=Conical limit points and uniform convergence groups
| journal=[[Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]]
| volume=1998
| date=1998
| issue=501
| pages=71–98
| doi=10.1515/crll.1998.081}}</ref> also independently obtained by [[Brian Bowditch|Bowditch]],<ref name=Bow-config /><ref name=Bow-topol>{{cite journal
| last1=Bowditch | first1=Brian H.
| title=A topological characterisation of hyperbolic groups
| journal=[[Journal of the American Mathematical Society]]
| volume=11
| date=1998
| issue=3
| pages=643–667
| doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-98-00264-1 | doi-access=free}}</ref> states:

A discrete convergence group action of a group <math>\Gamma</math> on a compact metrizable space <math>M</math> is uniform if and only if every non-isolated point of <math>M</math> is a conical limit point.

=== Word-hyperbolic groups and their boundaries ===

It was already observed by Gromov<ref>{{cite book
| author-link=Mikhail Gromov (mathematician) | first=Mikhail | last=Gromov
| chapter=Hyperbolic groups
| title=Essays in group theory
| pages=75–263
| series=Mathematical Sciences Research Institute Publications
| volume=8
| publisher=Springer
| location=New York
| year=1987
| doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-9586-7_3 | doi-access=free
| mr=919829
| editor-last=Gersten
| editor-first=Steve M.
| isbn=0-387-96618-8 }}</ref> that the natural action by translations of a [[word-hyperbolic group]] <math>G</math> on its boundary <math>\partial G</math> is a uniform convergence action (see<ref name=Bow-config /> for a formal proof). Bowditch<ref name=Bow-topol /> proved an important converse, thus obtaining a topological characterization of word-hyperbolic groups:

'''Theorem.''' Let <math> G</math> act as a discrete uniform convergence group on a compact metrizable space <math>M</math> with no isolated points. Then the group <math>G</math> is word-hyperbolic and there exists a <math>G</math>-equivariant homeomorphism <math>M\to \partial G</math>.

== Convergence actions on the circle ==

An isometric action of a group <math>G</math> on the [[hyperbolic plane]] <math>\mathbb H^2 </math> is called [[Geometric group action|''geometric'']] if this action is properly discontinuous and cocompact. Every geometric action of <math>G</math> on  <math>\mathbb H^2 </math> induces a uniform convergence action of <math>G</math> on <math>\mathbb S^1 =\partial H^2\approx \partial G</math>.
An important result of Tukia (1986),<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Tukia | first1=Pekka | authorlink1=Pekka Tukia
| title=On quasiconformal groups
| journal=[[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]]
| volume=46
| date=1986
| pages=318–346
| doi=10.1007/BF02796595 | doi-access=}}</ref> [[David Gabai|Gabai]] (1992),<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Gabai | first1=Davis | authorlink1=David Gabai
| title=Convergence groups are Fuchsian groups
| journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]
| series=Second series
| volume=136
| date=1992
| issue=3
| pages=447–510
| doi=10.2307/2946597
| jstor=2946597| url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183657188 }}</ref> Casson–Jungreis (1994),<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Casson | first1=Andrew
| last2=Jungreis | first2=Douglas
| title=Convergence groups and Seifert fibered 3-manifolds
| journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]
| volume=118
| date=1994
| issue=3
| pages=441–456
| doi=10.1007/BF01231540 | bibcode=1994InMat.118..441C
| doi-access=}}</ref> and Freden (1995)<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Freden | first1=Eric M.
| title=Negatively curved groups have the convergence property I
| journal=Annales Academiae Scientiarum Fennicae
| series=Series A
| volume=20
| date=1995
| issue=2
| pages=333–348
| url=https://www.acadsci.fi/mathematica/Vol20/freden.pdf
| access-date=September 12, 2022}}</ref> shows that the converse also holds:

'''Theorem.''' If <math>G</math> is a group acting as a discrete uniform convergence group on <math>\mathbb S^1</math> then this action is topologically conjugate to an action induced by a geometric action of <math>G</math> on <math>\mathbb H^2</math> by isometries.

Note that whenever <math>G</math>  acts geometrically on <math>\mathbb H^2 </math>, the group <math>G</math> is [[virtually]] a hyperbolic surface group, that is,  <math>G</math> contains a finite index subgroup isomorphic to the fundamental group of a closed hyperbolic surface.

== Convergence actions on the 2-sphere ==

One of the equivalent reformulations of [[Cannon's conjecture]], (posed by [[James W. Cannon]],<ref>{{cite book
| last1=Cannon | first1=James W.
| chapter=The theory of negatively curved spaces and groups
| title=Ergodic theory, symbolic dynamics, and hyperbolic spaces (Trieste, 1989)
| pages=315–369
| publisher=Oxford Sci. Publ., Oxford Univ. Press, New York
| date=1991
| chapter-url=http://mmontee.people.sites.carleton.edu/Cannon_Negatively_Curved.pdf
| access-date=September 12, 2022}}</ref> 
although an earlier and more general conjecture, reducing to the Cannon conjecture for compact type, was given by [[Gaven J. Martin]] and Richard K. Skora  <ref>{{Citation
 last1=Martin | first1=Gaven J.
| last2=Skora | first2=Richard K. 
| title=Group Actions of the 2-Sphere
| journal=[[American Journal of Mathematics]]
| volume=111
| pages=387–402
| publisher=The Johns Hopkins University Press
| date=1989
}}</ref>) 

These conjectures are in terms of word-hyperbolic groups with boundaries homeomorphic to <math>\mathbb S^2</math>, says that if <math>G</math> is a group acting as a discrete uniform convergence group on <math>\mathbb S^2</math> then this action is topologically conjugate to an action induced by a [[Geometric group action|geometric action]] of <math>G</math> on <math>\mathbb H^3</math> by isometries. These conjectures still remains open.

== Applications and further generalizations ==

* Yaman gave a characterization of [[relatively hyperbolic group]]s in terms of convergence actions,<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Yaman | first1=Asli
| title=A topological characterisation of relatively hyperbolic groups
| journal=[[Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]]
| volume=2004
| date=2004
| issue=566
| pages=41–89
| doi=10.1515/crll.2004.007}}</ref> generalizing Bowditch's characterization of word-hyperbolic groups as uniform convergence groups.
* One can consider more general versions of group actions with "convergence property" without the discreteness assumption.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Gerasimov | first1=Victor
| title=Expansive convergence groups are relatively hyperbolic
| journal=[[Geometric and Functional Analysis]]
| volume=19
| date=2009
| issue=1
| pages=137–169
| doi=10.1007/s00039-009-0718-7 | doi-access=}}</ref>
* The most general version of the notion of [[Cannon–Thurston map]], originally defined in the context of Kleinian and word-hyperbolic groups, can be defined and studied in the context of setting of convergence groups.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Jeon | first1=Woojin
| last2=Kapovich | first2=Ilya | authorlink2=Ilya Kapovich
| last3=Leininger | first3=Christopher
| last4=Ohshika | first4=Ken'ichi
| title=Conical limit points and the Cannon-Thurston map
| journal=Conformal Geometry and Dynamics
| volume=20
| date=2016
| issue=4
| pages=58–80
| arxiv=1401.2638
| doi=10.1090/ecgd/294  | doi-access=free}}</ref>
